The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

derivations.claim: If $P\not\ll Q$, choose E_0 with $Q(E_0)=0<P(E_0)$. Since $\phi^{-1}$ is measurable, $\phi(E_0)=(\phi^{-1})^{-1}(E_0)$ is measurable; then $\phi_\#Q(\phi(E_0))=0<\phi_\#P(\phi(E_0))$. Both divergences are $+\infty$ by [F1].

If $P\ll Q$, let $r=dP/dQ$. [given]
The function $s=r\circ\phi^{-1}$ is measurable. For every B in F,
$$\int_Bs\,d(\phi_\#Q)=\int_{\phi^{-1}(B)}r\,dQ=P(\phi^{-1}(B))=\phi_\#P(B),$$
so s is a Radon–Nikodym density of $\phi_\#P$ with respect to $\phi_\#Q$. By [F2], the push-forward integral identity applies separately to the nonnegative functions $(\ln s)^+$ and $(\ln s)^-$; the negative-part integrals are finite by [F1]. Therefore
$$D(\phi_\#P\|\phi_\#Q)=\int(\ln s)^+d(\phi_\#P)-\int(\ln s)^-d(\phi_\#P)=\int(\ln r)^+dP-\int(\ln r)^-dP=D(P\|Q),$$
including the case where the positive-part integral is $+\infty$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

For fixed $z$, [F2] gives the probability measure $\Pi_z$. [F2, given]
If $A\in\mathcal E$ and $B\in\mathcal F$, then
$$\Pi_z(A\times B)=K(z,A)L(z,B),$$
which is a measurable function of z by the two kernel assumptions in [F1]. Also $\Pi_z(E\times F)=1$ for every z.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the class of product-measurable $C\subseteq E\times F$ for which $z\mapsto\Pi_z(C)$ is measurable. Step 1.1 shows every rectangle belongs to $\mathcal D$, and the whole product does as well. If $C\in\mathcal D$, then $\Pi_z(C^c)=1-\Pi_z(C)$, so $C^c\in\mathcal D$. If $C_j$ are pairwise disjoint members, then $\Pi_z(\bigcup_j C_j)=\lim_n\sum_{j=1}^n\Pi_z(C_j)$ by countable additivity, a pointwise limit of measurable functions. Thus $\mathcal D$ is a lambda-system.

Rectangles are a pi-system generating $\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F$, so [F3] implies $\mathcal D=\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F$. Every section $\Pi_z$ is a probability by step 1.1; hence z↦$\Pi_z$ is the claimed probability kernel. All constructions are pointwise and use no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $M(z,\cdot)=K(z,\cdot)\otimes L(z,\cdot)$ is a probability kernel into the standard-Borel product of the X and Y spaces. Apply [F2] with base law $P_Z$ and kernel M. It gives a unique probability law R and the displayed rectangle formula; taking $C$ equal to the whole Z space shows its Z marginal is $P_Z$. The same rectangle identity is the conditional-law identity for M given Z.

Let $K',L'$ be alternative versions. By [F3], there are P_Z-null sets $N_X,N_Y$ such that $K(z,\cdot)=K'(z,\cdot)$ for $z\notin N_X$ and $L(z,\cdot)=L'(z,\cdot)$ for $z\notin N_Y$. Their product measures agree for every $z$ outside $N_X\cup N_Y$. Thus the two joint laws have the same rectangle values $R(C\times A\times B)$ for every measurable C,A,B; [F4] then makes the laws equal. This establishes version independence.

derivations.claim: First suppose $P\ll Q$ and $D(P\|Q)<\infty$. For bounded measurable $f$, let $Z_f=\int e^f\,dQ$ and define $Q_f$ by $dQ_f=e^f Z_f^{-1}dQ$. Then $Q_f$ is a probability equivalent to $Q$, and $dP/dQ_f=(dP/dQ)Z_fe^{-f}$. Taking logarithms and integrating under $P$ gives $D(P\|Q_f)=D(P\|Q)-\Phi_{P,Q}(f)$. By [F2], $\Phi_{P,Q}(f)\le D(P\|Q)$. If $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$ or $P\not\ll Q$, this upper bound is automatic.

If $P\not\ll Q$, choose a measurable $A$ with $Q(A)=0<P(A)$. For $f_t=t\mathbf1_A$, $\int e^{f_t}dQ=1$ and $\Phi_{P,Q}(f_t)=tP(A)\to+\infty$. Thus the bounded-function supremum is $+\infty=D(P\|Q)$ in the singular case.

Suppose $P\ll Q$, let $r=dP/dQ$, and set $\ell=\log r$ on $\{r>0\}$, with $\ell=-\infty$ on $\{r=0\}$; the latter set is P-null. Define $f_n=\max(-n,\min(n,\ell))$, taking $f_n=-n$ on $\{r=0\}$. The negative part of $\ell$ is integrable by [F1]; its clipped negative parts converge by [F4], while the clipped positive parts increase to $\ell^+$ and converge in integral by [F4]. Hence $\int f_n\,dP\to D(P\|Q)$, including value $+\infty$. Pointwise, $e^{f_n}\to r$ Q-a.e. and $0\le e^{f_n}\le r+1$, so [F4] gives $\int e^{f_n}dQ\to\int r\,dQ=1$. Therefore $\Phi_{P,Q}(f_n)\to D(P\|Q)$ and the bounded-function supremum is at least the divergence.

Fix a finite measurable partition $(A_i)_{i=1}^m$ and put $p_i=P(A_i)$, $q_i=Q(A_i)$. > ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\Phi_{P,Q}(f):=\int f\,dP-\ln\int e^f\,dQ.$$
Then
$$D(P\|Q)=\sup_{f\ {\rm bounded\ measurable}}\Phi_{P,Q}(f).$$
Equivalently, for every finite measurable partition $\mathcal P=(A_1,\ldots,A_m)$ of the whole space,

The union $\mathcal U=\bigcup_n\mathcal G_n$ is an algebra. The class of $A\in\mathcal G$ approximable in $\rho$-measure by a set in $\mathcal U$ is a sigma-algebra: complements preserve the symmetric-difference measure, finite unions preserve approximation, and for a countable union one first truncates it using continuity from below [F5] of the finite measure $\rho$, then approximates the finite union. Hence every set in $\mathcal G$ is approximable. Approximating bounded measurable functions first by simple functions and then their level sets gives bounded $\mathcal U$-measurable functions converging in $L^1(\rho)$, with one $\mathcal G_n$ containing each finite simple approximation. The approximants may be clipped to the same bound M. On that bound, [F2]'s variational functional is continuous under $L^1(\rho)$ approximation: $e^t$ is Lipschitz on $[-M,M]$, and the exponential integral is bounded below by $e^{-M}$. By [F2] applied to $P,Q$ and their restrictions to each $\mathcal G_n$, the supremum over all bounded $\mathcal G_n$-measurable functions is $D(P|_{\mathcal G_n}\|Q|_{\mathcal G_n})$. These test classes increase, so the restricted divergences increase; the approximation shows their supremum equals the unrestricted variational supremum $D(P\|Q)$. Hence $D(P\|Q)=\lim_n D(P|_{\mathcal G_n}\|Q|_{\mathcal G_n})$.

By [F1], countable generating algebras exist; their first-n finite Boolean subalgebras yield increasing finite quantizers by labeling their atoms. For the quantizers in the Statement, the same generated-sigma property is assumed, so in either case $\sigma(q_n(X),r_n(Y))$ increases to the product sigma-algebra of $(X,Y)$. Under the map $(x,y)\mapsto(q_n(x),r_n(y))$, the push-forward of $P_X\otimes P_Y$ is $P_{q_n(X)}\otimes P_{r_n(Y)}$, as is checked on rectangles of the finite output sets. Since $\sigma(q_n(X),r_n(Y))$ consists exactly of preimages of output events, every bounded measurable test function on that sigma-algebra factors through the finite output map. Therefore its restricted KL equals the KL of the push-forward laws, which by [F3] is $I(q_n(X);r_n(Y))$. Applying step 1.1 proves the ordinary mutual-information limit.

For the conditional statement, put $\mathcal G_n=\sigma(Z,q_n(X),r_n(Y))$. These sigma-algebras increase to the full product sigma-algebra of $(Z,X,Y)$ because the entire Z sigma-algebra is retained. A bounded $\mathcal G_n$-measurable simple function factors through $(Z,q_n(X),r_n(Y))$: each level set is the preimage of a measurable output set, and finitely many output sets can be made disjoint without changing their preimages. $K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For

$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $Z$, and let $K,L:Z\rightsquigarrow E$ be supplied probability kernels. Define their **conditional KL divergence with base $\mu$** by
$$D_\mu(K\|L):=\int_Z D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))\,\mu(dz)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The integrand is measurable by [[thm-conditional-kl-is-measurable]], so this is a well-defined nonnegative extended integral. No absolute-continuity assumption is imposed on individual fibers; a singular fiber has divergence $+\infty$. Changing supplied kernel versions on a $\mu$-null set does not change the integral.

measurable space and $\nu\ll\mu$, then the Radon–Nikodym class
$d\nu/d\mu$ has a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative. Every
finite-valued representative of that class is nonnegative

u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Assume there is an increasing measurable exhaustion $(X_n)$ with $ igcup_nX_n=X$, $\mu(X_n)<+\infty$, and $|
u|(X_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$. If $
u\ll\mu$, then there exists a measurable real-valued function $f$, unique up to $\mu$-almost-everywhere equality, such that
$$
u(E)=\int_Ef\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$

u|(X)<+\infty$, then $f\in L^1(\mu)$.

$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$

$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$

of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for

monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.
Every finite product of standard Borel spaces, with its finite product sigma-algebra, is standard Borel.

$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz)$$
exists uniquely on the product sigma-algebra and does not depend on the chosen versions of $K,L$. It has $Z$ marginal $P_Z$ and conditional law $M$ for $(X,Y)$ given $Z$.

$$R(C\times A\times B)=\int_C K(z,A)L(z,B)\,P_Z(dz).$$
Its existence, uniqueness, and independence of the versions K,L are established in [[lem-same-marginal-conditional-product-law-well-defined]]. Define the **conditional mutual information** by
$$I(X;Y\mid Z):=D(P_{XYZ}\|R)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The reference R has the same Z marginal as the joint law and makes X,Y independent conditionally on Z. The logarithm is natural, so finite values are measured in nats under [[def-it-information-units-and-logarithm-base]]. The definition is a divergence between full probability laws; it does not subtract two possibly infinite entropies.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space

of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let K,L be probability kernels from a measurable space $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ into a standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal E)$. Then $z\mapsto D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))$ is $\mathcal Z$-measurable, with $+\infty$ allowed. Consequently the integral used to define conditional KL is well-defined.

Let $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $Z$, and let $K,L:Z\rightsquigarrow E$ be supplied probability kernels. Define their **conditional KL divergence with base $\mu$** by
$$D_\mu(K\|L):=\int_Z D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))\,\mu(dz)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The integrand is measurable by [[thm-conditional-kl-is-measurable]], so this is a well-defined nonnegative extended integral. No absolute-continuity assumption is imposed on individual fibers; a singular fiber has divergence $+\infty$. Changing supplied kernel versions on a $\mu$-null set does not change the integral.

Assume AC only for the interface to the published general definition [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]. Let $p,q$ be probability vectors on a finite set $S$, and let $P(A)=\sum_{i\in A}p_i$, $Q(A)=\sum_{i\in A}q_i$ on $\mathcal P(S)$. Then the measurable-space divergence $D(P\|Q)$ equals the finite KL sum $\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i)$, with value $+\infty$ exactly when some $p_i>0=q_i$.

For a finite nonempty set identified with $[k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}$, a **probability vector** is $p=(p_i)_{i=1}^k$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; it is the outcome-weight vector of a finite probability space ([[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]). Its Shannon entropy in natural units is
$$H(p):=-\sum_{i=1}^k p_i\ln p_i,$$
with $0\ln0:=0$. For probability vectors $p,q$ on the same set $[k]$, the relative entropy is
$$D(p\|q):=\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln(p_i/q_i),$$
with value $+\infty$ if $p_i>0=q_i$ for some $i$. A matrix $A\in[0,1]^{N\times m}$ is **row-stochastic** when each row sums to one. For a probability row vector $p$ on $[m]$ and a row vector $X\in[0,1]^m$, the dot product $pX^{\mathsf T}=\sum_{i=1}^m p_iX_i$ is the acceptance probability under distribution $p$.

These definitions use finite sets only; entropy is between $0$ and $\ln k$, as proved where needed below.

Write $\ln$ for the natural logarithm $\log$ of [[def-natural-logarithm]]. Unless a base is displayed, every information quantity on this page uses $\ln$ and is measured in **nats**. For a base $b>1$ and $t>0$, define
$$\log_b t:=\frac{\ln t}{\ln b}.$$
The denominator is positive: $b>1$, $\ln$ is strictly increasing, and $\ln 1=0$ by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]. A base-$b$ entropy or divergence is obtained by replacing each $\ln$ in the finite formulas below by $\log_b$; use $0\log_b0:=0$ and assign $+\infty$ to a positive numerator over a zero denominator. derivations.claim: By [F2], the restriction $P_Z$ is a probability and $P_Z(\{0\})=0$. On each finite target set, define distance 0 on equal points and 1 on distinct points; distinct endpoints force at least one intermediate distance to be 1, so the triangle inequality holds. Tolerance $1/2$ makes every Cauchy sequence eventually constant; the whole finite set is dense, and radius-$1/2$ balls are singletons, so the space is complete and discrete, hence Polish and standard Borel by [F1]. The product target is standard Borel by the finite-product supplier in [F1]. For any Borel $C\subseteq[0,1]$ and $A\subseteq\{0,1\}$, replacing $\delta_0$ by $K'$ changes $\int_C K(z,A)P_Z(dz)$ only at $z=0$, a null point. Thus both K and K' satisfy the conditional-law integral identity for X given Z; the constant kernel L satisfies it for Y, and $J(z)=\delta_{(0,0)}$ satisfies it for $(X,Y)$. These kernels are measurable because their only nonconstant set of values is the Borel singleton $\{0\}$.

Let $J(z)=\delta_{(0,0)}$ be a conditional law of $(X,Y)$ given Z. With the original kernels, $K(z)\otimes L(z)=\delta_{(0,0)}$ for every z, so the pointwise KL is zero. With the alternative kernels, the product is $\delta_{(1,0)}$ at z=0 and $\delta_{(0,0)}$ for z>0. The joint law $P_{ZXY}$ and the conditional-product reference law built from K,L agree. K' equals K $P_Z$-almost everywhere, so [F3] says the reference law built from K',L' is the same law. Consequently both versions give $I(X;Y\mid Z)=D(P_{ZXY}\|P_{ZXY})=0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**

For a random element $X$ with law $P_X$, define its **law entropy** by
$$H(X):=I(X;X)=D(P_{XX}\|P_X\otimes P_X),$$
where $P_{XX}$ is the joint law of the diagonal pair $(X,X)$. This is an extended nonnegative quantity in nats and depends only on the law of X.

Let X have a probability law P on a standard-Borel space. Let $S=\{x:P(\{x\})>0\}$ be its set of atoms. Then S is countable. If $P(S)=1$ and its atom masses are $(p_i)$, the law entropy from [[def-law-entropy-as-self-mutual-information]] is
$$H(X)=\sum_i p_i\ln\frac1{p_i},$$
with value $+\infty$ allowed. If $P(S)<1$, then $H(X)=+\infty$.

For a probability law with Lebesgue density $f$ on $\mathbb R^d$, its **differential entropy**, when the integral is defined, is
$$h(f):=-\int_{\mathbb R^d} f(x)\ln f(x)\,dx.$$
This density-based quantity is not the law entropy $H(X)=I(X;X)$ of [[def-law-entropy-as-self-mutual-information]]. Differential entropy may be finite or negative even when law entropy is infinite; the uniform law on $[0,1]$ is a basic example. No identity between the two is used in this page.

([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]). Its
**nonnegative Lebesgue integral** is
$$\int f\,d\mu:=\sup\left\{\int s\,d\mu:\ s \text{ is nonnegative simple and } 0\le s\le f\right\},$$
where the simple integral on the right is the one from
[[def-integral-of-a-nonnegative-simple-function]].

The set of admissible simple minorants is nonempty because it contains the zero
function, which is simple ([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]).

derivations.claim: Define $P(A)=\lambda_1(A)$ for Borel $A\subseteq[0,1]$. By [F1], these sets are Lebesgue measurable and the restricted measure is countably additive; the box formula gives $P([0,1])=1$, so P is a probability. For each $x\in[0,1]$, the degenerate interval $[x,x]=\{x\}$ has measure $x-x=0$. Thus every singleton has P-mass zero, and the atomic set $S=\{x:P(\{x\})>0\}$ is empty.
The identity map on $[0,1]$ has law P, and its value space is standard Borel by [F2]. Since $P(S)=0<1$, [F3] gives $H(X)=+\infty$.

Extending the density by zero outside $[0,1]$ gives $f=\mathbf1_{[0,1]}$. On the interval $f\ln f=1\ln1=0$, and off the interval the integrand is zero by the convention in [F4]. Thus $f\ln f$ is the zero function on $\mathbb R$; its integral is zero by [F4], so the differential entropy is $h(f)=0$.
